question: Ainsley controls [General Ferrous Rokiric]. What happens when they cast [Illusion]?
answer:
Nothing triggers — as printed in the card data, Illusion is a **token** creature (0/2 blue Illusion), and a token isn't a card and isn't cast. Tokens are *created* by an effect, so Ainsley never "casts Illusion" at all, and General Ferrous Rokiric's ability, which reads "Whenever you cast a multicolored spell, create a 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token," never sees a cast event and doesn't trigger.

Secondary point, in case the intent was a blue Illusion *spell* rather than the token: General Ferrous Rokiric only triggers on **multicolored** spells — spells that are two or more colors. Illusion as given has a color identity of blue only, so even a hypothetical monocolored blue Illusion spell would not trigger General Ferrous Rokiric and would produce no Golem token.

A related trap from the rules provided: if the Illusion in question were one half of a split card, only the characteristics of the half actually being cast exist while it's on the stack — the other half's characteristics are treated as though they didn't exist [709.3b]. So even though a split card is the combination of both halves' mana costs (and therefore possibly multicolored) in every zone except the stack [709.4], [709.4b], casting a monocolored half yields a monocolored spell that would not trigger General Ferrous Rokiric.

Also worth noting for the board state: General Ferrous Rokiric has "Hexproof from monocolored," which protects it from being targeted by monocolored spells and abilities — but the Illusion token's ability ("Whenever this creature blocks a creature, that creature doesn't untap during its controller's next untap step") doesn't target, so if the Illusion token blocks General Ferrous Rokiric, that ability applies normally and General Ferrous Rokiric won't untap during Ainsley's next untap step.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more: General Ferrous Rokiric's trigger cares only about spells its controller casts, so the number of opponents doesn't change anything.

question:
Aydan casts [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded], and Nico answers by casting [Spell Queller], exiling Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with its triggered ability.
When Spell Queller leaves the battlefield, can Aydan choose to cast [Birthright Boon] or do they have to cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded?
answer:
Aydan may choose either one — he can cast Birthright Boon (the Adventure half) or Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (the creature half), and either way it's cast without paying its mana cost.

Why:

- An adventurer card has two sets of characteristics: the inset frame on the left gives the alternative (Adventure) characteristics the object may have while it's a spell, and the normal characteristics appear as usual [715.2]. As a player plays an adventurer card, that player chooses whether to play it normally or as an Adventure [715.3]. That choice is made each time the card is cast, so being cast as Kellan, the Fae-Blooded the first time doesn't lock Aydan in.
- Spell Queller's ability lets the exiled card's owner cast that card "without paying its mana cost." That normally shuts off alternative costs [Spell Queller ruling #6], but casting a card as an Adventure is expressly not casting it for an alternative cost, and effects that let you cast a spell without paying its mana cost may be applied to the Adventure [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #9]. So Birthright Boon is a legal choice and costs nothing.
- Timing: Aydan must cast it right then, as part of the resolution of Spell Queller's leaves-the-battlefield ability; he can't hold it for later. Timing permissions based on the card's type are ignored, so the fact that Birthright Boon is a sorcery doesn't stop him from casting it at instant speed during that resolution [Spell Queller ruling #2].
- The new spell has no relation to the original Kellan, the Fae-Blooded spell that was exiled; nothing from that first casting carries over [Spell Queller ruling #1].
- Follow-up if he picks Birthright Boon: when Birthright Boon resolves, Aydan exiles it instead of putting it into the graveyard, and for as long as it stays exiled he may later cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded as a permanent spell [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #6] — but that later casting follows normal timing (main phase, empty stack) and costs {2}{R} [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon ruling #5].

Player count doesn't change this: Spell Queller's ability refers to the exiled card's owner, so Aydan makes the choice whether the game is two-player or multiplayer. Note also that the exile check was legal in the first place because the spell cast was Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with mana value 3, which is 4 or less.

question: Can Nicolas cast [Memory Lapse] targeting Aubrianna's [Underworld Charger] that is escaping from their graveyard?
answer:
Yes. Once Aubrianna finishes casting Underworld Charger with its escape ability, Underworld Charger is a creature spell on the stack, and spells on the stack are legal targets for Memory Lapse, which says "Counter target spell" [115.2]. Escape is just an alternative way to cast the card from the graveyard ("Escape [cost]" means "You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost"), so an escaped spell is countered exactly like any other spell [702.138a].

Timing detail: Nicolas can't respond to the act of casting itself. Once Aubrianna begins casting Underworld Charger it immediately moves to the stack, and no player can take actions until the casting is complete [Underworld Charger ruling #1]. After that, Nicolas gets priority and can cast Memory Lapse targeting Underworld Charger.

Result: Memory Lapse cancels Underworld Charger and removes it from the stack; it doesn't resolve, so it never enters the battlefield and it never gets its two +1/+1 counters [701.6a]. Instead of going to Aubrianna's graveyard, Underworld Charger is put on top of Aubrianna's library, because Memory Lapse's self-replacement effect changes that destination before anything else can [Memory Lapse]. Notably, this means Underworld Charger can't simply escape again from the graveyard — Aubrianna has to draw it first. (The Memory Lapse ruling that flashback overrides the library destination applies only to flashback; escape has no such replacement, so top of library it is [Memory Lapse ruling #1].) The escape cost Aubrianna already paid, including the three cards exiled from her graveyard, is not refunded.

The rules provided here don't distinguish two-player from multiplayer games for this interaction: any opponent (or any player) with priority who can legally cast Memory Lapse may target the escaping Underworld Charger, so the answer is the same at a two-player or a larger table.

question: Ariyah has [Guardian Naga] in their graveyard. Can they flash back Guardian Naga's Adventure with [Flashback]?
answer:
No. Ariyah can't target Guardian Naga with Flashback, so they can't flash back Banishing Coils (Guardian Naga's Adventure).

Why: an adventurer card's Adventure text (here, Banishing Coils, an Instant — Adventure) is only a set of *alternative* characteristics printed in the inset frame, and those characteristics exist only while the card is on the stack having been cast as an Adventure [715.2]. In every other zone — including Ariyah's graveyard — the card has only its normal characteristics [715.4]. Per the Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils rulings, an adventurer card is a permanent card in every zone except the stack, and you ignore its alternative characteristics there. So in the graveyard it is simply Guardian Naga, a creature card with mana cost {5}{W}{W}.

Flashback says "Target instant or sorcery card in your graveyard gains flashback until end of turn." A creature card is not a legal target, so Flashback can't be cast targeting Guardian Naga at all (and if it somehow were already on the stack, it would fail for having no legal target).

Two further points even in a hypothetical where targeting worked: Flashback sets the flashback cost equal to the card's mana cost, which for Guardian Naga in the graveyard is {5}{W}{W} (five generic plus two white), not Banishing Coils' {2}{W}; and per the Flashback rulings, flashback only permits casting "if the resulting spell is an instant or sorcery spell," which a Guardian Naga creature spell would not be.

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players — nothing here depends on player count.

question: Ace controls [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker] and activates its ability, turning it into a creature. They then play a second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker. What happens when the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves?
answer:
The legend rule applies: Ace must choose one of the two Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker permanents to keep, and the other is put into its owner's graveyard.

Why: the first Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is currently a legendary 4/4 red Dragon creature (its first ability makes it a legendary creature; it keeps its name and the supertype legendary), and the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker enters the battlefield as a legendary planeswalker with four loyalty counters. The legend rule is a state-based action that only cares about (a) legendary supertype, (b) same name, and (c) same controller \u2014 it does not care that one is a creature and the other is a planeswalker [704.5j].

Timing: the moment the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker finishes resolving, a player would receive priority, so the game checks state-based actions first and the legend rule is applied immediately \u2014 Ace can't respond in between or use both [117.5] [704.3].

Which one to keep is Ace's free choice [704.5j]:
- Keep the animated one: it stays a 4/4 flying, indestructible, hasty Dragon until end of turn (it reverts to a planeswalker afterward, keeping whatever loyalty counters it has). The newly cast Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker goes to the graveyard.
- Keep the newly cast one: it's a planeswalker with 4 loyalty whose ability can be activated on a later turn. The animated Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker goes to the graveyard \u2014 note that indestructible does not help here, because the legend rule puts the permanent into the graveyard rather than destroying it [704.5j].

Multiplayer: no difference. The legend rule is evaluated per player \u2014 "controlled by the same player" \u2014 so it works identically at a two-player or a larger table, and opponents controlling their own Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker are unaffected [704.5j].

question: Ainsley controls [Reconnaissance] and attacks Nancy with [Loxodon Wayfarer]. After combat damage is dealt, can Ainsley use Reconnaissance's activated ability to untap Loxodon Wayfarer?
answer:
Yes — as long as Ainsley activates it while the combat phase is still going on (i.e., in the combat damage step after damage is dealt, or in the end of combat step), Reconnaissance can target Loxodon Wayfarer, remove it from combat, and untap it. Damage already dealt is not undone.

Why: Loxodon Wayfarer became an attacking creature when it was declared as an attacker, and it "remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first" [508.1k], [Attacking Creature]. Dealing combat damage does not end that status. So after the combat damage step, Loxodon Wayfarer is still a legal target for Reconnaissance's "{0}: Remove target attacking creature you control from combat and untap it." Reconnaissance's own reminder text confirms this timing: "If you activate during end of combat, the creature will untap after it deals combat damage."

Once the ability resolves, Loxodon Wayfarer is removed from combat and stops being an attacking creature [506.4b]. That's purely retroactive-free: it doesn't take back the damage already dealt to Nancy, and per the Reconnaissance ruling it doesn't undo anything that triggered on the declaration of attackers or blockers [Reconnaissance ruling #1].

Timing assumption and the other reading: I'm assuming Ainsley still has priority within the combat phase. If Ainsley instead waits until the combat phase has ended (e.g., the postcombat main phase), Loxodon Wayfarer is no longer an attacking creature [508.1k], so there is no legal target and the ability can't be activated for that purpose.

Player count doesn't matter here: the rules cited apply the same whether Nancy is Ainsley's only opponent or one of several players, since Reconnaissance only cares that Loxodon Wayfarer is an attacking creature Ainsley controls.

question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
answer:
Yes — Arjun can do it, by using Thermopod's mana ability during the cost‑payment window to put a creature card into the graveyard first.

How it works step by step:

1. Arjun announces the activation of Molten‑Tail Masticore's ability "{4}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: This creature deals 4 damage to any target." The ability goes on the stack as its own object and targets are chosen at that time [602.2a], [602.2b].
2. The total cost is locked in: {4} in generic mana (payable with any color or colorless mana) plus the additional cost of exiling a creature card from the graveyard [601.2h], [602.2b].
3. Because the total cost includes a mana payment, Arjun now gets a window to activate mana abilities before costs are actually paid [601.2g]. Thermopod's "Sacrifice a creature: Add {R}" is a mana ability, so Arjun activates it, sacrificing a nontoken creature. That creature card goes to the graveyard as part of paying Thermopod's cost, and Arjun gets {R}.
4. Now Arjun pays the total cost [601.2h]: {4} generic (the {R} from Thermopod can pay one of those four generic), and exiles the creature card that just arrived in the graveyard.

Notes on which creature to sacrifice:
- Thermopod can sacrifice itself to its own ability; Thermopod is a nontoken card, so it lands in the graveyard and can then be exiled to pay Molten‑Tail Masticore's cost.
- Arjun could even sacrifice Molten‑Tail Masticore itself to Thermopod and then exile Molten‑Tail Masticore from the graveyard. Once activated, the ability exists on the stack independently of its source; removing the source doesn't affect it, and the game uses last known information, so the ability still deals 4 damage [113.7a].
- Sacrificing a token wouldn't help — a token isn't a card and won't be in the graveyard to exile.

Timing assumption: this all happens inside the single activation, in the mana‑ability window of rule [601.2g], after the cost is determined but before it's paid. If Arjun instead tried to announce the activation with an empty graveyard and never used Thermopod, they'd be unable to pay the exile cost and the activation would be illegal and rewound [602.2].

Player count doesn't matter here: every action is taken by Arjun alone, so the answer is the same in a two‑player game or at a multiplayer table (the only multiplayer wrinkle is which opponent or permanent is chosen as the target of the 4 damage).

question: Can Ashley pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast [Beseech the Queen] or is Ashley limited to only paying {B}{B}{B} to do so?
answer:
Ashley can pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B}. Ashley is not limited to {B}{B}{B}.

So choosing the "two mana" half of each of the three symbols and paying each with two black mana is perfectly legal — that's the {6} option in the card's own ruling, funded entirely with black mana [Beseech the Queen ruling #1].

question: Arielle has [Blessed Hippogriff] in their graveyard. Arielle casts [Mission Briefing], can they choose to cast the adventure of Blessed Hippogriff?
answer:
No. While Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing is in Arielle's graveyard, it is not an instant or sorcery card, so Mission Briefing can't choose it at all.

An "adventurer" card like Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing has two sets of characteristics: the normal ones (the creature Blessed Hippogriff, {3}{W}) and the alternative ones printed in the inset frame (the Adventure, Tyr's Blessing, {W} Instant — Adventure) [715.2]. Those alternative Adventure characteristics only apply while the card is a spell on the stack that was cast as an Adventure. In every other zone — including the graveyard — the card has only its normal characteristics [715.4], meaning it's a creature card there, as confirmed by the Adventure ruling that an adventurer card is a permanent card in every zone except the stack and that you ignore its alternative characteristics in those cases [Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing ruling #8].

Mission Briefing instructs you to "choose an instant or sorcery card in your graveyard," and Blessed Hippogriff // Tyr's Blessing doesn't meet that description in the graveyard, so it's not a legal choice — even though Tyr's Blessing would be an instant if the card were on the stack cast as an Adventure. Note also that Mission Briefing doesn't change timing permissions for what you do cast [Mission Briefing ruling #4].

This works the same way regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on the number of opponents, since Mission Briefing only looks at the caster's own graveyard.

question: Neriah controls [Cliffhaven Sell-Sword]. Ari casts [Oubliette] targeting it. Will Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phase back in at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step?
answer:
No. Cliffhaven Sell-Sword will not phase in during Neriah's untap step. Oubliette phases it out "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield," so Cliffhaven Sell-Sword stays phased out for as long as Oubliette remains on the battlefield, and it phases in immediately after Oubliette leaves the battlefield (tapped, per Oubliette's text) [Oubliette ruling #6].

Why: "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist — it can't be targeted, can't attack or block, its static abilities do nothing, and its triggered abilities can't trigger [Oubliette ruling #5]. Normally, phasing is a static ability that works during the untap step: in each player's untap step, before the active player untaps, that player's phased-in permanents with phasing phase out and their phased-out permanents phase in [702.26a]. But Cliffhaven Sell-Sword doesn't have the phasing ability — it was phased out by a one-shot "until" effect. Rule [610.4a] specifically says a permanent phased out "until" a specified event does not phase in as a result of the untap step turn-based action; instead, a second one-shot effect created immediately after the specified event (here, Oubliette leaving the battlefield) phases it in.

Two small notes:
- Technically it's Oubliette's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability that targets Cliffhaven Sell-Sword, not the spell itself. If Oubliette leaves the battlefield before that trigger resolves, Cliffhaven Sell-Sword is never phased out or tapped at all [Oubliette ruling #1].
- Another effect could still phase Cliffhaven Sell-Sword in early; if that happens, the "phase in when Oubliette leaves" one-shot effect no longer happens [610.4a].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the duration keys off Oubliette leaving the battlefield, not off whose untap step it is, and the untap-step phasing action in [702.26a] only concerns permanents with the phasing ability.

question: Nico controls [Lazav, the Multifarious], which is currently a copy of [Lazav, Dimir Mastermind]. Abram discards [Kasimir the Lone Wolf] due to hand size at the end of their turn. Lazav, the Multifarious's ability triggers. After it resolves, what is Lazav, the Multifarious named?
answer:
After the trigger resolves, the permanent is named **Lazav, Dimir Mastermind**.

Here's the chain. Nico's Lazav, the Multifarious had used its {X} ability to become a copy of the card Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, "except its name is Lazav, the Multifarious, it's legendary..., and it has this ability." So at that point the permanent's copiable values were the printed values of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind (3/3, hexproof, and Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability) with the name and ability exceptions baked in — copy effects can include modifications, and the modified values become the copiable values [707.9b].

That means the permanent now has Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability: "Whenever a creature card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, you may have Lazav become a copy of that card, except its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has hexproof and this ability." Abram discarding Kasimir the Lone Wolf to hand size puts a creature card into an opponent's graveyard from hand, which is covered by "from anywhere," so that ability triggers.

When it resolves and Nico accepts, the permanent becomes a new copy of Kasimir the Lone Wolf with the exceptions written in that ability — and those exceptions set the name to Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, not Lazav, the Multifarious. Note that the {X} ability of Lazav, the Multifarious is gone — the new copy effect replaced the copiable values, and only hexproof and "this ability" (the Dimir Mastermind trigger) were carried along. question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
answer:
Alivia can cast either half — Road or Ruin.

Why the card is a legal target: in every zone other than the stack (here, the graveyard), a split card's characteristics are those of both halves combined, so Road // Ruin is both an instant card and a sorcery card [709.4, 709.4c]. Torrential Gearhulk's trigger targets "target instant card in your graveyard," and Road // Ruin qualifies because of the instant half.

Why either half is castable: Alivia chooses which half to cast before putting it on the stack, and only that half is evaluated and put on the stack [709.3, 709.3a]. Torrential Gearhulk is an effect that allows casting the card from the graveyard, and the Road // Ruin rulings state that if another effect allows you to cast a split card with aftermath from a graveyard, you may cast either half — including the aftermath half [Road // Ruin ruling #7].

Practical points:
- Either half is cast without paying its mana cost (so neither Road's {2}{G} nor Ruin's {1}{R}{R} is paid). Additional costs would still have to be paid, and any {X} would be 0 [Torrential Gearhulk ruling #2, Torrential Gearhulk ruling #3].
- The card must be cast right then, during the resolution of Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability; Alivia can't hold it for later in the turn [Torrential Gearhulk ruling #1].
- If Alivia casts Ruin, it needs a legal target creature, and the card will be exiled when it leaves the stack whether it resolves or is countered — both from aftermath and from Torrential Gearhulk's replacement effect [Road // Ruin ruling #6]. If Alivia casts Road instead, Torrential Gearhulk's replacement effect exiles it instead of putting it into the graveyard.

One assumption: I'm reading the trigger as targeting Road // Ruin itself while it sits in Alivia's graveyard. Nothing here depends on the number of players — only Alivia's own graveyard is involved — so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table (the provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific text bearing on this).

question: Alvaro controls [Draugr Thought-Thief] and [Lotusguard Disciple]. Nico controls [Sands of Time] and [Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]. If Alvaro casts [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats], can they choose to only have the cost reduced by {1}?
answer:
No. Alvaro's party has two creatures, so Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats is reduced by exactly {2}; the reduction isn't optional and can't be scaled down.

Why: a player's party consists of up to one Cleric, up to one Rogue, up to one Warrior, and up to one Wizard that player controls, and the game calculates that number automatically — players never designate which creatures are "in" their party and can't exclude creatures to lower the count [700.8a] [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #3]. Alvaro controls Draugr Thought-Thief (Zombie Rogue, so the Rogue check is yes) and Lotusguard Disciple (Bird Cleric, so the Cleric check is yes); no Warrior and no Wizard, so the count is 2 [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #5]. Neither creature has two party types here, so the "count for the highest result" rule doesn't change anything [700.8b].

Total cost: start with the mana cost {4}{B}{R}, add any cost increases, then apply the reduction of {1} per party creature — {2} total. That comes off only the generic portion, so Alvaro pays {2}{B}{R}. The colored {B} and {R} symbols are untouched, and Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats still has mana value 6 regardless of what was actually paid [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #4].

Nico's Sands of Time and Yurlok of Scorch Thrash are irrelevant to the party count — party only counts creatures the spell's controller controls, and neither of those is a creature Alvaro controls (Yurlok of Scorch Thrash is a Lizard Shaman anyway, not a party type) [700.8a]. This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, since party is measured per player from their own creatures.

question: Adriel controls [Oko, Thief of Crowns], [Gilded Goose], and a Food token. Adriel uses Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability to make the Food token into a 3/3 Elk. Can Adriel then sacrifice it to Gilded Goose?
answer:
No. Once Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability resolves on the Food token, that token is no longer a Food, so Gilded Goose's "{T}, Sacrifice a Food: Add one mana of any color" ability can't be activated by sacrificing it.

Why:

1. Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 makes the target lose all abilities and become a green Elk creature with base power and toughness 3/3. Per the Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling, this overwrites all colors and creature types and the permanent "loses any other card types it has (such as artifact)" [Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #5]. So the token is now just a creature, not an artifact.

2. Food is an artifact type (an artifact subtype), never a creature type [Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #13] [Gilded Goose ruling #2]. Rule 205.1a says that when an object's card type is removed, subtypes correlated with that card type remain only if they're also subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise they're removed for as long as that card type is gone. Since the token is no longer an artifact and Food isn't a creature type, the Food subtype falls off. Its new creature type is Elk.

3. Gilded Goose's cost says "Sacrifice a Food." Under rule 109.2, a description using a subtype without the words "card," "spell," or "source" means a permanent of that subtype on the battlefield — i.e., a permanent that is currently a Food. The 3/3 Elk isn't one, so it can't pay that cost.

Also note the token lost all abilities, so it no longer has its own "{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: You gain 3 life" ability either.

Timing: I'm assuming Adriel resolved the +1 first and is asking about sacrificing afterward. If instead Adriel sacrifices the token to Gilded Goose first (or in response, while Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability is still on the stack), it's still a Food at that moment and the sacrifice works fine — and Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability would then be countered for having an illegal target if that token was its only target.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it plays out the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Natasha controls a [Lifeline] and 2 [Scarwood Goblins]. Adriel casts [Plague Wind]. Does Lifeline trigger and return the creatures to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step?
answer:
Short answer: Lifeline does trigger twice (once for each Scarwood Goblin), but whether anything comes back depends entirely on whether any creature is still on the battlefield when those triggers resolve — and Plague Wind only spares creatures Adriel controls.

**Why it triggers.** Lifeline reads "Whenever a creature dies, if another creature is on the battlefield, return the first card to the battlefield under its owner's control at the beginning of the next end step." Both Scarwood Goblins die simultaneously to Plague Wind ("Destroy all creatures you don't control"). A "dies" trigger is a leaves-the-battlefield trigger, and those "look back in time": the game uses the appearance of objects immediately before the event to decide whether the ability triggers [603.10a]. Immediately before Plague Wind finished resolving, each Scarwood Goblin had another creature (the other Scarwood Goblin) on the battlefield, so Lifeline triggers once for each of them.

**Why they may still not come back.** "if another creature is on the battlefield" is an intervening "if" clause: the condition is checked when the ability would trigger *and again as the ability resolves*; if it's false on resolution the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing [603.4] [608.2a]. Lifeline's own ruling states this exact case: if more than one creature is on the battlefield and they all go to the graveyard at once, none of them are returned, because there must be at least one creature on the battlefield when the ability resolves [Lifeline ruling #5].

So:
- **If Adriel controls no creatures** (and no other creature survives), both Scarwood Goblins are the last creatures on the battlefield. Both Lifeline triggers are removed from the stack on resolution, no delayed "at the beginning of the next end step" effects are ever created, and neither Scarwood Goblin returns.
- **If Adriel controls at least one creature** (Plague Wind doesn't destroy Adriel's own creatures), that creature satisfies the "another creature is on the battlefield" check on resolution. Both triggers resolve, each setting up its own delayed return, and the two Scarwood Goblins return under Natasha's control at the beginning of the next end step — one at a time, since Lifeline triggered separately for each [Lifeline ruling #4]. Each Scarwood Goblin only returns if that card is still in the graveyard at that time [Lifeline ruling #2]. Note also that Lifeline itself is an artifact, so Plague Wind never touches it; and even if Lifeline had left the battlefield after triggering, the triggers would still work [Lifeline ruling #3].

**Timing assumption:** I'm treating both Scarwood Goblins as dying simultaneously during Plague Wind's resolution, which is how Plague Wind works. If instead they had died at different times (say, one already destroyed earlier in the turn), the earlier death's trigger would see the surviving Scarwood Goblin and resolve fine, and only the final creature's trigger would be at risk of fizzling.

**Multiplayer:** Plague Wind is worded from Adriel's perspective, so with more than two players it destroys every creature that Adriel doesn't control — every other player's creatures, not just Natasha's. That doesn't change the analysis; it just means the only creatures that can satisfy Lifeline's intervening "if" on resolution are Adriel's. And because Lifeline works for all players, it will also trigger for the other players' dying creatures.

question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?
answer:
Chalice of the Void counters the original Stream of Thought, but Alfred still gets both replicate copies, and those two copies resolve normally.

How it plays out:

1. Casting. Alfred pays Stream of Thought's mana cost {U} plus its replicate cost {2}{U}{U} twice, for a total of {4}{U}{U}{U}{U}{U} (four generic plus five blue). Replicate is an additional cost: "As an additional cost to cast this spell, you may pay [cost] any number of times," plus a triggered ability that copies the spell for each payment [702.56a]. Paying it doesn't change Stream of Thought's mana cost, so the spell on the stack still has mana value 1.

2. Two abilities trigger on the cast: Alfred's replicate trigger, and Nico's Chalice of the Void trigger ("Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters on this artifact, counter that spell") — Stream of Thought's mana value 1 matches Chalice of the Void's one charge counter.

3. Ordering. Because Stream of Thought is a sorcery, it's Alfred's turn, so Alfred is the active player. In APNAP order Alfred puts his replicate trigger on the stack first, then Nico puts the Chalice of the Void trigger on top of it [101.4, 603.3b]. So the Chalice of the Void trigger resolves first and counters Stream of Thought, putting it into Alfred's graveyard.

4. The copies still happen. "You'll copy Stream of Thought for each time you paid its replicate cost, even if it's countered" [Stream of Thought ruling #4]. When the replicate trigger resolves, it creates two copies on the stack, and Alfred may choose new targets for either copy [702.56a, 707.10].

5. The copies aren't countered. Copies created by replicate are put directly onto the stack and are not cast [707.10, Stream of Thought ruling #5], so Chalice of the Void's ability — which only triggers on a spell being cast — doesn't trigger on them, even though each copy also has mana value 1.

6. Resolving the copies. Each copy makes its target player mill four cards, and Alfred shuffles up to four cards from his graveyard into his library. Note a quirk here: normally the copies resolve before the original, so they can't shuffle Stream of Thought itself back in [Stream of Thought ruling #3], but because Chalice of the Void already countered the original, Stream of Thought is sitting in Alfred's graveyard when the copies resolve — so he can shuffle that very card into his library with one of the copies.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Chalice of the Void was already on the battlefield with its counter when Alfred cast Stream of Thought. If Chalice of the Void entered or gained/lost counters only after the spell was cast, its ability wouldn't have triggered at all [Chalice of the Void ruling #1] and the original Stream of Thought would resolve too (after the copies).

Multiplayer note: with more than two players the result is the same — all nonactive players' triggers are placed after Alfred's in turn order [101.4], so Nico's Chalice of the Void trigger still ends up above the replicate trigger and resolves first. The only extra freedom is that Alfred may aim each copy at a different opponent (or himself) when choosing new targets.

question: Adrienne attacks with [Sporeweb Weaver], and Nicolas blocks it with [Serpent Assassin]. Can Nicolas use [Tishana's Tidebinder] to counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability?
answer:
Yes. Nicolas can target Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability with Tishana's Tidebinder, because Tishana's Tidebinder targets the ability on the stack, not the permanent Sporeweb Weaver.

Why hexproof from blue doesn't stop it:
- "Hexproof from blue" means Sporeweb Weaver can't be the target of blue spells opponents control or abilities opponents control from blue sources [Sporeweb Weaver ruling #1]. Hexproof of any kind is worded as a restriction on targeting *that permanent* [702.11b].
- An ability on the stack is its own object, separate from the permanent that produced it [109.1], and once it has triggered it exists on the stack independently of its source [113.7a]. Abilities are legal targets precisely because they're objects that can't exist on the battlefield [115.2].
- So Tishana's Tidebinder's enters-the-battlefield trigger legally targets the "whenever this creature is dealt damage" trigger even though Sporeweb Weaver itself is untargetable by Nicolas's blue spells and abilities.

Assumed timing: Serpent Assassin's combat damage is dealt in the combat damage step, Sporeweb Weaver's damage trigger goes on the stack at the next priority, and Nicolas then flashes in Tishana's Tidebinder while that trigger is still on the stack. That's the only window — if Nicolas casts Tishana's Tidebinder before combat damage (say, during declare blockers), there is no triggered ability on the stack yet to target, and the Sporeweb Weaver trigger will resolve normally later.

Result if it resolves: Sporeweb Weaver's trigger is countered, so Adrienne gains no life and gets no Saproling token. Additionally, because Sporeweb Weaver is still a creature on the battlefield when Tishana's Tidebinder's trigger resolves (Serpent Assassin's 2 damage doesn't kill the 1/4), Sporeweb Weaver loses all abilities — including reach, hexproof from blue, and the damage trigger — for as long as Tishana's Tidebinder remains on the battlefield [Tishana's Tidebinder ruling #2]. Note that if Sporeweb Weaver had died from the damage, the trigger would still be countered, but nothing would lose abilities [Tishana's Tidebinder ruling #3].

Player count doesn't matter: hexproof from blue restricts targeting by spells and abilities of opponents generally, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
answer:
Tempted by the Oriq will do nothing: Insurrection resolves first and makes Autumn the controller of every creature, so both Soldier tokens stop being creatures "that player controls" for Breanna and Case. Both targets are illegal, so Tempted by the Oriq doesn't resolve and is put into Autumn's graveyard.

How it plays out:

1. Casting Insurrection at that moment is only legal because of Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born's Cosmic Awareness — "As long as an opponent has cast a spell this turn, you may cast spells as though they had flash." Insurrection is a sorcery, and the stack isn't empty while Tempted by the Oriq is on it, so this works only if Breanna, Case, or another opponent has already cast a spell this turn. If no opponent has cast a spell this turn, Autumn simply can't cast Insurrection there.

2. Insurrection, cast second, resolves first (the stack resolves last-in, first-out; that ordering rule isn't in the provided context, but it's the standard stack behavior). It untaps all creatures, Autumn gains control of all of them until end of turn, and they all gain haste — including Breanna's Soldier token and Case's Soldier token (Insurrection ruling: you untap all creatures, control all creatures, and give all creatures haste).

3. Tempted by the Oriq then tries to resolve. Its targeting requirement is "target creature or planeswalker that player controls with mana value 3 or less," checked again on resolution: a spell rechecks the legality of its targets, and changes to the game state (here, a change of controller) can make a target illegal; if every target for every instance of "target" is illegal, the spell doesn't resolve and goes to its owner's graveyard [608.2b]. Since Autumn now controls both Soldier tokens, neither is a creature Breanna controls or a creature Case controls, so both targets are illegal and Tempted by the Oriq is removed from the stack.

4. Net result: Autumn controls and can attack with both Soldier tokens this turn (they have haste from Insurrection), but Insurrection's control effect ends at end of turn, so the tokens go back to Breanna and Case during the cleanup step. Autumn loses out on Tempted by the Oriq's permanent theft — that spell's control-changing effect would have lasted indefinitely (Tempted by the Oriq ruling).

Assumed timing / the other order: I'm assuming Insurrection was cast while Tempted by the Oriq was still on the stack, as described. If instead Autumn had let Tempted by the Oriq resolve first and then cast Insurrection, Tempted by the Oriq would have taken both Soldier tokens indefinitely, and Insurrection's temporary control of them afterward would be redundant — Autumn would keep them permanently.

Partial-illegality note: [608.2b] only counters the spell if all targets are illegal. If, say, only Breanna's token had changed controllers and Case's had not, Tempted by the Oriq would still resolve and steal Case's token permanently.

Player count: this scenario already involves at least three players (Autumn plus opponents Breanna and Case), and Tempted by the Oriq targets once "for each opponent." In a two-player game there'd be only one target, and Insurrection making that single target illegal would likewise cause Tempted by the Oriq to be removed from the stack with no effect.

question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
answer:
Yes — Amelia can cast both instants, one under each Aminatou's Augury.

Why: each Aminatou's Augury is a single ability that both exiles cards and then refers to "the exiled cards." An ability that both causes objects to be affected and refers back to those same objects is linked to itself [607.1, 607.1c], so each copy of Aminatou's Augury grants permission only for the cards that that particular Aminatou's Augury exiled. The "one spell of each nonland card type" allowance is therefore tracked separately per resolution — it is not a shared, once-per-turn cap.

So the first Aminatou's Augury lets Amelia cast one artifact and one instant from among its eight exiled cards; the second Aminatou's Augury independently lets Amelia cast one instant (and one of each other nonland type) from among its own exiled cards. Neither Aminatou's Augury's permission reaches the other's exiled pile.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both Aminatou's Augury spells are cast in the same turn. Each Aminatou's Augury's permission lasts only "until end of turn," so if the second Aminatou's Augury were cast on a later turn, the first Aminatou's Augury's instant would no longer be castable from exile and only the second instant could be cast. Also, normal timing rules still apply to the spells cast this way [Aminatou's Augury ruling: "You must follow the normal timing permissions and restrictions of each spell you cast"], though instants can be cast whenever Amelia has priority, and casting an exiled card moves it out of exile so it can't be cast again [Aminatou's Augury ruling: "Casting an exiled card causes it to leave exile. You can't cast it multiple times"].

Player count doesn't matter here: the provided rules contain nothing that changes this between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

question: Agustin casts [Seasoned Pyromancer] and has two other cards in hand, one of which is a land card. Nico controls [Leyline of the Void]. How many tokens are created?
answer:
One 1/1 red Elemental token.

How it plays out: Seasoned Pyromancer's enters-the-battlefield ability makes Agustin discard two cards, then draw two cards, then create a token for each nonland card discarded this way. Discarding means moving a card from its owner's hand to that player's graveyard [701.9a]. Agustin is an opponent of Nico, who controls Leyline of the Void, so its replacement effect ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") applies: both discarded cards are exiled rather than reaching Agustin's graveyard.

Those cards were still discarded, and Seasoned Pyromancer's ability can still see them. Exile is a public zone, and although an object that changes zones is normally a new object with no memory of its past, an effect that moves an object to a public zone can still find that object [400.7j]. Leyline of the Void's own ruling confirms this: abilities that check whether a card was discarded still work, and spells or abilities that check the characteristics of the discarded card can find that card in exile [Leyline of the Void ruling #3].

Agustin discarded exactly two cards, one of which was a land card, so only one nonland card was discarded this way — one Elemental token. Agustin still draws two cards.

Multiplayer note: Leyline of the Void only replaces cards going to the graveyards of Nico's opponents, so the answer is the same at a two-player table or a bigger one, as long as Agustin is an opponent of Nico. If Agustin were Nico's teammate (or Nico himself), the cards would hit the graveyard normally and the token count would be unchanged anyway — still one.

question: Aranza controls a [Welding Jar] enchanted by Nico's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Aranza's upkeep, Nico casts [Word of Seizing] to take control of the Welding Jar. What happens as the trigger resolves?
answer:
Aranza takes 2 damage from Curse Artifact. Because Word of Seizing has already resolved and Nico controls Welding Jar, Aranza cannot sacrifice Welding Jar when Curse Artifact's trigger resolves, so the "unless" clause fails and Curse Artifact deals 2 damage to Aranza.

Why:

- Curse Artifact's trigger reads "deals 2 damage to that player unless they sacrifice that artifact." Rule 118.12a says "[Do something] unless [a player does something else]" means the same as "[A player may do something else]. If [that player doesn't], [do something]." So the sacrifice is an optional cost Aranza may pay on resolution of the trigger; if it isn't paid, the damage happens (118.12).
- Rule 701.21a: a player can't sacrifice a permanent they don't control. Word of Seizing gave Nico control of Welding Jar until end of turn, so Aranza — the player the trigger is targeting for damage, since she was the enchanted artifact's controller at the beginning of her upkeep — has no legal way to pay. Nico is not offered the choice; only the player named by the trigger can pay it.
- Word of Seizing's split second (and [Word of Seizing ruling #6]) means that once Word of Seizing was on the stack, Aranza could only take mana abilities and certain special actions — she could not activate Welding Jar's "Sacrifice this artifact: Regenerate target artifact" ability in response. Also, casting Word of Seizing didn't alter Curse Artifact's already-triggered ability ([Word of Seizing ruling #5]); that trigger just resolves and, with the cost unpayable, deals the damage.

question: Alina controls a [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle] and 5 [Mountain]s. They plays a 6th Mountain and target Nico with Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger. In response, Nico activates [Memorial to War], targeting the Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle. Will they be dealt 3 damage?
answer:
Yes — Nico still takes 3 damage (if Alina chooses to have the damage dealt), even though Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle is destroyed first.

Why:

1. Once a triggered ability is on the stack it exists independently of its source. Destroying or otherwise removing the source after that point doesn't affect the ability, and where the ability says the source does something ("you may have this land deal 3 damage to any target"), the game uses the source's last known information — the source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists [113.7a]. So Memorial to War destroying Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle in response does not counter or fizzle the trigger.

2. The intervening 'if' clause is still satisfied. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's ability checks the condition twice: when the Mountain enters (Alina controlled 5 other Mountains, so it triggered) and again on resolution — it does nothing if Alina controls fewer than five Mountains other than the one that entered [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #4]. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle is not itself a Mountain, so destroying it doesn't lower the Mountain count; Alina still controls the 5 other Mountains, and the condition is met. (Compare [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #2]: only a Mountain leaving the battlefield changes that count.)

3. Nico was targeted when the ability triggered; Alina decides whether to actually have the damage dealt as the ability resolves, since the ability says "you may" [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #1]. If Alina says yes, Nico is dealt 3 damage.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nico activated Memorial to War ({4}{R}, {T}, Sacrifice Memorial to War) while Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger was already on the stack, so Memorial to War's land-destruction resolves first. If instead Nico had somehow destroyed Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle before the 6th Mountain entered, the ability would never have triggered at all and no damage would occur.

Player count: nothing here changes with more than two players — Nico was chosen as the target when the ability triggered, and that target is unaffected by how many opponents are at the table. (The provided rules don't include any multiplayer-specific rule that would alter this.)

question: Arely equips [Barbed Batterfist] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
answer:
No — Champion of the Flame does not die. With Barbed Batterfist attached, Champion of the Flame is a 4/2.

The math: Champion of the Flame is printed 1/1. Its own static ability gives it +2/+2 for each Aura and Equipment attached to it, and Barbed Batterfist is one Equipment attached to it, so that's +2/+2. Barbed Batterfist itself says the equipped creature gets +1/-1. Both are power/toughness modifications from static abilities, which apply together in layer 7c; they're cumulative and the order they're applied in doesn't matter (see [613.5], where multiple layer 7c effects simply add together). 1/1 + 2/+2 + 1/-1 = 4/2.

Since Champion of the Flame's toughness is 2 (greater than 0), the state-based action check that happens whenever a player would receive priority finds nothing to do to it ([704.3]). It only dies if it has 2 or more damage marked on it at that check — but a 1/1 Champion of the Flame with any damage marked would already have been destroyed before you equipped, so in the normal case there's no marked damage and it survives.

Timing note: I'm assuming Barbed Batterfist is attached with no damage already marked on Champion of the Flame. If Champion of the Flame somehow already had damage marked (for example, it was pumped earlier in the turn and took 2+ damage), attaching Barbed Batterfist raises its toughness to 2 but marked damage stays on it, and it would be destroyed at the next state-based action check if that damage is 2 or more ([704.3]).

The converse warning on Champion of the Flame's ruling matters later: if Barbed Batterfist is unattached, destroyed, or moved to another creature during the turn, Champion of the Flame drops back toward 1/1 and previously nonlethal marked damage can become lethal [Champion of the Flame ruling #1].

One aside on Barbed Batterfist: if it was equipping the 2/2 Rebel token it created, you can pay its equip cost of {1} (as a sorcery) to move it to Champion of the Flame; the Rebel token stays on the battlefield and returns to 2/2 [Barbed Batterfist ruling #1].

The provided rules here are not player-count dependent, so this answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aviana controls a [Meng Huo's Horde] and a [Deathrite Shaman]. Nico controls a [Propaganda]. Can Aviana use Deathrite Shaman's ability to pay for the Meng Huo's Horde to attack?
answer:
No. Aviana cannot use Deathrite Shaman's first ability to produce the mana for Propaganda's attack cost.

Why:

1. Propaganda's cost is an additional cost on the declaration of the attacker, paid during the declare attackers step at the moment attackers are declared, not an ability that can be activated later [Propaganda ruling #3][Propaganda ruling #4]. Attacking with Meng Huo's Horde while Nico's Propaganda is on the battlefield requires paying {2} (two generic mana, payable with mana of any color or colorless).

2. Declaring attackers is a turn-based action with a fixed sequence: the active player declares attackers and chooses optional costs [508.1g], the total cost is locked in [508.1h], the active player may then activate mana abilities [508.1i], and finally pays all costs — partial payment is not allowed [508.1j]. The only thing Aviana may do inside that window to make mana is activate a mana ability.

3. Deathrite Shaman's first ability ({T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.) is not a mana ability, because it requires a target [605.1a][Deathrite Shaman ruling #2]. It uses the stack and can be responded to, so it cannot be activated during the mana-ability window in 508.1i.

4. Could Aviana just activate Deathrite Shaman earlier, in the beginning of combat step, and hold the mana? No — each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and that mana is lost [106.4]. Mana made during the beginning of combat step is gone before the declare attackers step begins [500.4]. And once the declare attackers step starts, the declaration happens as a turn-based action before anyone gets priority, so there is no chance to resolve a non-mana ability first.

So Aviana needs {2} from some other source (a real mana ability, a mana-producing land, etc.) to attack Nico with Meng Huo's Horde. Note that Deathrite Shaman's second and third abilities don't make mana at all, so they're irrelevant here.

Timing note: I'm assuming Aviana wants to activate Deathrite Shaman as part of, or immediately before, declaring attackers. If instead she activated it at some earlier point in the same step in which attackers are declared — which is impossible for the declare attackers step, since the declaration is the first thing that happens — the mana would still have to survive to the payment; mana made in any prior step is emptied.

Multiplayer: Propaganda reads "Creatures can't attack you...," so the {2} is owed only for creatures attacking Nico. In a two-player game that means every attack. With three or more players, Aviana can attack a different opponent (or a planeswalker/battle they control, if any) with Meng Huo's Horde and owe Propaganda nothing.

question: Amos casts [Rise from the Grave] targeting [Rhizome Lurcher] in their graveyard. Assuming there are no other cards in any graveyards, how many +1/+1 counters will Rhizome Lurcher enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rhizome Lurcher enters the battlefield with one +1/+1 counter.

Why: Rhizome Lurcher's undergrowth ability reads "This creature enters with a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard." An "enters with..." ability is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield, and the number is determined as the permanent enters, using the game state at that moment [614.1c] [614.12]. At that moment Rhizome Lurcher itself is still counted — the card's own ruling states that if you return Rhizome Lurcher from your graveyard to the battlefield, its undergrowth ability counts itself [Rhizome Lurcher ruling #3]. Since the problem states no other cards are in any graveyard, the count is exactly 1, so Rhizome Lurcher enters as a 3/3 (2/2 plus one +1/+1 counter).

Rise from the Grave also makes Rhizome Lurcher a black Zombie in addition to its other colors and types; that doesn't change the counter count, and it only adds black and Zombie rather than overwriting Fungus Zombie or its green/black colors [Rise from the Grave ruling #3].

Assumption and multiplayer note: I'm assuming Rhizome Lurcher is in Amos's own graveyard (as the question says "their graveyard"). Rise from the Grave can target a creature card in *any* graveyard, which matters at a table with more than two players just as it does with two: if Rhizome Lurcher were instead coming out of an opponent's graveyard, "your graveyard" in the undergrowth ability would mean Amos's graveyard (Amos controls Rhizome Lurcher as it enters), Rhizome Lurcher would not be counting itself, and with no other cards anywhere it would enter with zero counters as a 2/2.

question: Ava controls [Undead Minotaur] enchanted with [Shade's Form]. Nico casts [Hour of Revelation] to destroy both Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Will Undead Minotaur return to the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — Undead Minotaur returns to the battlefield under Ava's control.

Why: Shade's Form reads "When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control." That is a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability (its trigger condition is a permanent going from the battlefield to a graveyard), and leaves-the-battlefield abilities are one of the listed exceptions where the game "looks back in time" [603.10a]. Instead of checking what exists after the event, the game uses the existence of the ability and the appearance of the objects immediately before the event. Immediately before Hour of Revelation destroyed everything, Shade's Form was on the battlefield attached to Undead Minotaur, so the ability triggers even though Shade's Form is put into the graveyard at the exact same time as Undead Minotaur [603.10a], [603.1].

Sequence: Hour of Revelation resolves and destroys all nonland permanents simultaneously, including Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Shade's Form's trigger goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, and when it resolves, the Undead Minotaur card is returned from the graveyard to the battlefield under the control of the ability's controller — Ava, who controlled Shade's Form. Shade's Form itself stays in the graveyard; it does not come back attached, so the returned Undead Minotaur is a fresh 2/3 with no Aura on it and no {B} pump ability.

One timing caveat: this assumes Shade's Form was still attached to Undead Minotaur at the moment Hour of Revelation resolved. If Shade's Form had already left the battlefield beforehand (for example, destroyed by an earlier spell), it would not be there to trigger, and Undead Minotaur would simply stay in the graveyard.

Player count doesn't matter here — the rules provided contain nothing that treats this differently at a multiplayer table than in a two-player game; the trigger belongs to Ava as Shade's Form's controller regardless of who cast Hour of Revelation.

(Side note on the spell's cost, not affecting the outcome: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}, and its own text reduces it by {3} — the generic portion only — if there are ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield, leaving {W}{W}{W}.)

question: Amara controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nehemiah casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
**Wayward Angel ends up as a black 6/6 Angel Horror creature with no abilities** (name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, mana value 6, still controlled by Amara).

Here's the layer-by-layer walkthrough, assuming the order stated in the question: Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield when Nehemiah's Humility resolved, so Humility has the later timestamp [613.7, 613.7a]. Wayward Angel's threshold ability is a single static ability whose effect has parts in several layers, and per [613.6] each part applies in its own layer — and once the effect starts applying, it keeps applying in the later layers even if the ability generating it gets removed along the way.

- **Layer 5 (color) [613.1e]:** Threshold is active (7+ cards in Amara's graveyard), so Wayward Angel "is black." This happens *before* Humility strips abilities in layer 6, so it sticks. Per [Wayward Angel ruling #1], Wayward Angel is black only, not white and black.
- **Layer 6 (abilities) [613.1f, 613.3]:** In timestamp order, Wayward Angel's threshold effect first grants trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature"; then Humility, with the later timestamp, removes *all* abilities from all creatures — flying, vigilance, trample, the upkeep trigger, and the threshold ability itself [Humility ruling #3]. Wayward Angel now has no abilities.
- **Layer 7b (setting P/T) [613.4, 613.4b]:** Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.
- **Layer 7c (modifying P/T) [613.4c]:** Two effects apply, and they simply add together (order doesn't matter): the threshold effect's +3/+3 still applies under [613.6] even though the ability was removed in layer 6, and Muraganda Petroglyphs gives +2/+2 because, as of layer 6, Wayward Angel is a creature with no abilities. 1/1 + 3/+3 + 2/+2 = **6/6**.

Muraganda Petroglyphs itself is unaffected — it's an enchantment, not a creature, so Humility doesn't touch it, and its static ability keeps working. Note also that per [Muraganda Petroglyphs ruling #1] any text at all counts as an ability, which is exactly why the +2/+2 only turns on once Humility has scrubbed Wayward Angel clean.

Timing caveat: if instead Wayward Angel had entered the battlefield *after* Humility resolved (later timestamp), then in layer 6 Humility would apply first and the threshold effect second, leaving Wayward Angel with trample and the sacrifice trigger. It would then have abilities, Muraganda Petroglyphs would not apply, and it would be a black 4/4 (1/1 base +3/+3) with trample and the upkeep trigger.

Player count doesn't matter here: Humility says "all creatures" and Muraganda Petroglyphs says "creatures," so both apply regardless of controller, and the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Nayeli controls [Trinisphere]. Ainsley casts [Noxious Revival], paying 2 life for the Phyrexian mana. What is the total cost of the Noxious Revival?
answer:
Ainsley pays {3} (three generic mana) plus the 2 life. Because Ainsley chose to pay 2 life for the Phyrexian symbol, the mana component of Noxious Revival's cost is nothing, so Trinisphere raises it to three mana — and that added mana is generic, payable with any colors or colorless mana [107.4f].

Why, step by step:
- {G/P} is a Phyrexian mana symbol: it can be paid with one green mana or by paying 2 life [107.4f].
- Ainsley announces the choice to pay 2 life while proposing the spell (the same point at which modes and X are chosen), which is before the total cost is calculated [601.2b], [Noxious Revival ruling #3].
- The total cost is then determined: mana cost, plus additional costs and increases, minus reductions, and then effects that directly affect the total cost are applied and the cost is locked in [601.2f]. Trinisphere is applied last, after all increases and reductions, if the mana component is less than three mana [Trinisphere ruling #1].
- With 2 life chosen, Noxious Revival's mana component is zero mana, which is less than three, so Trinisphere makes it three mana. Locked-in total cost: {3} and 2 life.

Note the alternative choice: if Ainsley had instead announced paying {G} for the Phyrexian symbol, the mana component would be one green mana, and Trinisphere would bring it to three mana as {2}{G} — the green requirement stays, only generic mana is added. Ainsley cannot switch after the cost is locked in [601.2f].

Also note Noxious Revival's mana value stays 1 regardless of what Ainsley actually paid [Trinisphere ruling #1].

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; Trinisphere affects each spell cast by any player, including Nayeli's own, and nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Anakin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Maritime Guard] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Anakin casts [Clever Impersonator], choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability as it enters the battlefield. They choose to enchant a [Balduvian Barbarians] in their graveyard. After Clever Impersonator's trigger resolves and returns the Balduvian Barbarians to the battlefield, Anakin activates the ability of the Clever Impersonator to turn it into a copy of Maritime Guard. What happens?
answer:
**The key step fails: Clever Impersonator cannot become a copy of Animate Dead, so Balduvian Barbarians is never returned. Clever Impersonator simply enters as a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces (with Mizzium Transreliquat's {1}{U}{R} ability), and the later activation then makes it a permanent copy of Maritime Guard.**

Step by step:

**1. What Clever Impersonator copies.** Clever Impersonator's replacement ability lets it enter as a copy of any nonland permanent, and when the chosen permanent is itself a copy, Clever Impersonator enters as whatever that permanent is copying [Clever Impersonator ruling #5], [707.2]. Mizzium Transreliquat used its second ability, which does not wear off and leaves it a copy of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1], and the results of all copy effects are copied [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #4]. So Clever Impersonator enters as a legendary 3/1 Sakashima of a Thousand Faces that also has the {1}{U}{R} "become a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability" ability. (Mizzium Transreliquat could legally target Sakashima of a Thousand Faces in the first place only because Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact.)

**2. The Sakashima choice is illegal.** Because Clever Impersonator enters as Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, Sakashima's own "as it enters" copy ability is active and can be applied [707.5], [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #1], [Clever Impersonator ruling #6]. But that ability reads "enter as a copy of **another creature you control**." Animate Dead is an Aura, and Mycosynth Lattice only makes permanents artifacts in addition to their other types — it does not make them creatures; an Aura would need something like March of the Machines to become a creature [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4]. Animate Dead is therefore an artifact enchantment Aura, not a creature, and is not a legal choice. Clever Impersonator stays a Sakashima of a Thousand Faces copy with the {1}{U}{R} ability. Note that if Anakin had wanted Animate Dead, Clever Impersonator's *own* ability ("any nonland permanent") could have chosen it — but that choice was spent on Mizzium Transreliquat.

**3. No Animate Dead trigger, no Balduvian Barbarians.** Since Clever Impersonator never becomes an Animate Dead, its enters-the-battlefield trigger never exists, nothing is enchanted, and Balduvian Barbarians stays in the graveyard.

**4. Legend rule.** Anakin now controls two permanents named Sakashima of a Thousand Faces (Mizzium Transreliquat and Clever Impersonator). Both copies include Sakashima's other ability, "The 'legend rule' doesn't apply to permanents you control," so neither is sacrificed [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #7].

**5. The activation on Maritime Guard.** Clever Impersonator has the {1}{U}{R} Mizzium Transreliquat ability, so it can target Maritime Guard — legal because Mycosynth Lattice makes Maritime Guard an artifact. Mycosynth Lattice's third ability lets Anakin pay the {U} and {R} with mana of any color (or colorless mana), though it removes no other restrictions on that mana [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1]. On resolution, Clever Impersonator permanently becomes a copy of Maritime Guard — a 1/3 Merfolk Soldier (an artifact and colorless because of Mycosynth Lattice) — except it keeps the {1}{U}{R} ability [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1]. It loses Sakashima's copy ability and legend-rule ability. It does **not** get -1/-0: Animate Dead is attached to the original Maritime Guard, and non-copy effects, counters, and Auras aren't copied [707.2], [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2], [Clever Impersonator ruling #10]. The original Maritime Guard, Animate Dead, and Mizzium Transreliquat-as-Sakashima are all unaffected.

**Timing note:** I'm assuming the Sakashima choice is attempted as Clever Impersonator enters (the only time it could be) and that the {1}{U}{R} activation happens afterward. If Anakin instead activated {1}{U}{R} on Maritime Guard while responding to something, the result is the same — the copy effect just applies at whatever point it resolves and doesn't wear off.

**Player count:** nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table; every effect involved affects only Anakin's own permanents or applies equally to everything on the battlefield.

question: Amare casts [Insatiable Hemophage] targeting [Canal Monitor] to mutate unto it. Can Nico cast [Withering Boon] to counter Insatiable Hemophage?
answer:
Yes. A mutating Insatiable Hemophage is still a creature spell, so Nico can target it with Withering Boon.

Why: mutate is a static ability that functions while the spell is on the stack; paying the mutate cost {2}{B} instead of Insatiable Hemophage's mana cost {3}{B} is just an alternative cost, and it makes the spell "a mutating creature spell" that targets a non-Human creature with the same owner — here, Canal Monitor [702.140a]. Nothing about that changes Insatiable Hemophage's card type: it is still a Creature spell on the stack. Withering Boon says "Counter target creature spell," and per its ruling a "creature spell" is any spell with the type Creature [Withering Boon ruling #2]. So Insatiable Hemophage is a legal target.

Costs for Nico: Withering Boon costs {1}{B} — one generic mana plus one black mana — and, as an additional cost to cast it, Nico must pay 3 life [Withering Boon ruling #1]. The life payment is part of casting, not part of resolution, so Nico pays it even if Withering Boon is later countered or its target becomes illegal.

If Withering Boon resolves and counters Insatiable Hemophage, Insatiable Hemophage never resolves, so it never mutates onto Canal Monitor and its "Whenever this creature mutates" ability never triggers — Canal Monitor is simply left alone as a 5/3 Lizard. Also note that Withering Boon targets the spell Insatiable Hemophage, not Canal Monitor; Canal Monitor being the mutate target is irrelevant to Withering Boon's legality.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table — any opponent with priority can respond. The only multiplayer-specific note in the provided material concerns Insatiable Hemophage's mutate trigger in Two-Headed Giant (the opposing team loses twice X while you gain X) [Insatiable Hemophage ruling #1], and that trigger never happens at all if Withering Boon counters the spell.

If you do, it becomes a mutating creature spell and targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as this spell.” Casting a spell using its mutate ability follows the rules for paying alternative costs (see 601.2b and 601.2f–h).

question: Amirah controls Azors Gateway with 4 different CMC cards exiled by it. They targets it with [Karn's Touch]. After that resolves, they activates [Azor's Gateway], and transforms it into [Sanctum of the Sun]. What are the characteristics of the new object after it has transformed?
answer:
After the transform, the permanent is Sanctum of the Sun, and it is a **legendary artifact land creature** with power and toughness each equal to its mana value (2), so a 2/2, and it still has Sanctum of the Sun's "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total" ability. It is untapped (the transform ability untaps it as part of resolution).

Why:

1. **The Karn's Touch effect survives the transform.** Transforming does not create a new object, and any effects that applied to the permanent continue to apply to it [712.18]. Karn's Touch's effect is a continuous effect with a fixed duration — until end of turn [611.1] — so it keeps applying to the same permanent even though the face-up face is now Sanctum of the Sun.

2. **Types stack rather than replace.** Karn's Touch says the permanent "becomes an artifact creature." An effect that makes something an "artifact creature" lets the object retain all of its prior card types, supertypes, and subtypes [205.1b]. Sanctum of the Sun is printed as a Legendary Land, so with Karn's Touch applied it is a Legendary Artifact Land Creature. It gains no creature subtype (Karn's Touch grants none), and it keeps its land status and therefore its mana ability, which is still a mana ability that doesn't use the stack [Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun].

3. **Power/toughness.** Karn's Touch sets power and toughness each equal to the permanent's mana value [Karn's Touch]. The mana value of this double-faced card is 2 (from the front face Azor's Gateway's {2} cost — two generic mana, no colored or {C} symbols), so Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 while Karn's Touch's effect lasts. Note the provided context doesn't include the general rule text for how a back face derives its mana value; I'm relying on the card data listing this card at MV 2.

4. **Summoning sickness / activating the ability.** Once Karn's Touch resolved, Azor's Gateway was a creature, so its {T} ability — and later Sanctum of the Sun's {T} mana ability — can only be activated if Amirah has continuously controlled that permanent since the beginning of their most recent turn; it doesn't matter how long it has been a creature [Karn's Touch ruling #1]. I'm assuming Amirah met that condition when they activated Azor's Gateway; if the permanent had come under their control this turn, that activation wouldn't have been legal in the first place. I'm also assuming the card drawn and exiled by that activation had a fifth distinct mana value, which is what enabled the life gain, untap, and transform [Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun].

At end of turn the Karn's Touch effect ends, and the permanent goes back to being just a Legendary Land named Sanctum of the Sun with no power or toughness.

None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
answer:
Nicholas chooses, and his legal choices are Onakke Ogre (which returns to the battlefield at the same time) or Aryana's Ascended Lawmage — but not Aryana's Cemetery Gate.

Why:

- Sudden Disappearance exiled every nonland permanent Nicholas controlled, which includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze itself (an Aura is a nonland permanent). At the beginning of the next end step the delayed trigger returns those cards to the battlefield under their owner's control, so Paralyze comes back under Nicholas's control.
- Because Paralyze is entering the battlefield by something other than resolving as an Aura spell, and Sudden Disappearance doesn't specify what it enchants, Nicholas chooses what Paralyze enchants as it enters, and the choice must be legal for its enchant creature ability and any other applicable effects [303.4f]. This is not targeting.
- Ascended Lawmage is a legal choice. Hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities its controller's opponents control [702.11b]; attaching an Aura on entry involves no targeting, so hexproof doesn't prevent Nicholas from choosing Ascended Lawmage. Paralyze's enters trigger would then tap Ascended Lawmage, and it wouldn't untap during Aryana's untap step unless Aryana pays {4} at the beginning of her upkeep.
- Cemetery Gate is not a legal choice. Paralyze is a black Aura (mana cost {B}), and a permanent with protection from black can't be enchanted by black Auras; if one somehow ended up attached, it would go to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [702.16c]. So Nicholas can't choose Cemetery Gate under rule 303.4f's "legal object" requirement.
- Onakke Ogre returns to the battlefield simultaneously with Paralyze, and it's an ordinary creature with no protection or other restriction, so it's the natural (and typical) choice. Note the provided rules don't include a specific rule text about attaching to permanents entering simultaneously; if your group rules that only creatures already on the battlefield count, Nicholas's only remaining option in the two-player setup described would be Ascended Lawmage.
- Any other creature on the battlefield is also a legal choice if it has no protection/other restriction. If Paralyze has no legal object to enchant at all, it can't enter attached to anything.

Multiplayer: the analysis is unchanged in substance. Sudden Disappearance targets a single player (Nicholas), so only his nonland permanents were exiled; with more than two players, Nicholas may also choose any legal creature controlled by any other player at the table, subject to the same protection restriction [702.16c] and the legality requirement of [303.4f].

question: Amaris controls [Eruth, Tormented Prophet] and, during their draw step, they attempt to dredge [Golgari Grave-Troll]. What happens?
answer:
Amaris gets to pick exactly one of the two replacement effects, and if they pick dredge, dredge is what happens: Amaris mills six cards and returns Golgari Grave-Troll from the graveyard to hand, and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect does nothing at all — no cards are exiled.

Why: both Eruth, Tormented Prophet ("If you would draw a card, exile the top two cards of your library instead") and Golgari Grave-Troll's dredge 6 ("if you would draw a card, you may instead mill six cards and return this card from your graveyard to your hand" — dredge functions only from the graveyard, per [702.52a]) are replacement effects trying to modify the same draw event. When two or more replacement effects would modify the same event, the affected player chooses which one to apply [616.1], and any of the applicable effects may be chosen [616.1e]. Amaris is the affected player, so Amaris chooses. Choosing dredge here is legal only if Amaris has at least six cards in their library; you can't announce dredge with fewer [702.52a] (Golgari Grave-Troll ruling: "You can't attempt to use a dredge ability if you don't have enough cards in your library").

Once dredge is applied, the draw event is replaced and never happens [614.6]. Eruth, Tormented Prophet's replacement effect was waiting to replace a draw that no longer occurs, so it simply doesn't do anything [614.7] — it does not get to also exile two cards, and it is not applied to the mill. Also, once Amaris announces they're applying dredge, no player can take actions until Golgari Grave-Troll is in hand and the six cards are milled (Golgari Grave-Troll ruling).

The other choice: if Amaris instead applies Eruth, Tormented Prophet, they exile the top two cards of their library and may play those cards this turn, the draw never happens, and dredge does nothing [614.6], [614.7]. Amaris may apply Eruth, Tormented Prophet even with fewer than two cards in library, exiling whatever is there and not losing the game for the attempted draw (Eruth, Tormented Prophet ruling).

Multiplayer note: only Amaris is the affected player here, so only Amaris chooses and the answer is identical at any table size. APNAP order [616.1] would matter only if multiple players had to make such choices simultaneously.
